subject: Science
theme: Global satellite navigation systems and space independence
question_short_text: Galileo Project: European satellite navigation system
text: What is the Galileo Project which has been in news recently?
options: An intercountry programme of missile shield developed by the United States of America
A Project developed by India with assistance from Canada
An environmental protection project being developed by Japan
A multi-satellite navigation project being developed by the European Union
answerText: (d) A multi-satellite navigation project being developed by the European Union
explanation: The Galileo Project is Europe's global navigation satellite system (GNSS), similar to the United States' GPS. It aims to provide accurate positioning, navigation, and timing services worldwide under civilian control.

research.summary: Galileo is a €10 billion European Union satellite navigation program developed jointly by the European Commission and the European Space Agency (ESA) to provide independent, civilian-controlled global positioning services. The project was conceived to reduce European dependence on the US-controlled GPS and Russian GLONASS systems, which could theoretically be disabled during geopolitical conflicts. By 2007—the year of this question—the project was in critical condition: the public-private partnership had collapsed in 2006, private investors had withdrawn, and the EU faced severe funding crises. However, on November 30, 2007, EU transport ministers unanimously approved the project and reallocated €3.4 billion from other budgets to ensure its continuance as a fully publicly-funded initiative. The first experimental satellite, GIOVE-A, was launched in December 2005, with a second test satellite (GIOVE-B) launched in April 2008. The system is designed to consist of 30 satellites in three medium earth orbits at 23,222 km altitude, orbiting at a 56-degree inclination to ensure global coverage. Unlike GPS, which offers military advantages to the US, Galileo is explicitly designed as a civilian system under 100% EU funding and control, though military users can access it. Initial services began in December 2016. The system provides meter-level accuracy and is particularly valuable for applications where redundancy matters—working in combination with GPS to enhance reliability, especially in environments where tall buildings or polar regions limit single-system coverage.
facts: Galileo initially struggled to gain funding and was described as 'almost dead' in January 2002 when private investors pulled out due to competition from free GPS services
The system's constellation will comprise 30 operational satellites plus spares positioned in three orbital planes at 23,222 km altitude for continuous global coverage
Galileo satellites orbit at 56° inclination, providing superior coverage at higher latitudes compared to other GNSS systems that use lower inclinations
Ground control centers are located in Fucino, Italy and Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany, making Galileo's infrastructure entirely European-controlled
India, Ukraine, and Morocco signed partnership agreements with the EU to participate in the Galileo program between 2004-2005
